newsitem.title: INDIA: Punjab polls set new agenda for Indian parties.
newsitem.headline: Punjab polls set new agenda for Indian parties.

text.p: The landslide victory for a Sikh-Hindu alliance in elections to India's Punjab state legislature should reduce pressure on Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front alliance, analysts said on Monday.

Foremost was the humiliating defeat of the farming state's ruling Congress party, they said. The once-monolithic Congress now governs only six of India's 26 states and has been reduced to a reluctant supporter of the country's fractious ruling centre-left coalition.
Congress won only 14 seats in Punjab's 117-seat legislature in Friday's election when final results were announced on Monday, a sharp reversal from the 87 seats it held.
The main Sikh Akali Dal party won 74 seats, and its ally in the state, the rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party won 18.
The analysts said Congress was expected to scale down its frequent threats to topple the United Front alliance, which took power last June, and force mid-term elections at the national level.

"The Congress will simply have to pause," said Surjit Grewal, a political analyst in Punjab's capital Chandigarh. "The lesson in Punjab is that the Congress is extremely unpopular here. The scene can't be much brighter for it in other regions."
An independent computer survey showed the Congress garnered only 27 percent of votes in Punjab. Its previous low was in 1980 when it won 33 percent of the vote.
"If the Congress wants to precipitate mid-term polls it should go ahead and bring down the Deve Gowda government," Grewal said. "I don't believe its people in parliament are so suicidal."

Reeling from a spate of corruption scandals and its worst-ever defeat in last year's national elections, the Congress replaced former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao as party president in September with veteran politician Sitaram Kesri.
Congress leaders tried to put a brave face on the Punjab result.
"There is no link between this result and Mr Kesri's leadership," said Ghulam Nabi Azad, a Congress general secretary handpicked by the party's new leader.
"There are other serious issues in the verdict that need to be looked at," Azad told state-run Doordarshan television.
Akali Dal leaders said the Punjab election also held a lesson for the BJP, their traditional rival and the main opposition group in the federal parliament.

"The BJP should now realise the benefits of having the support of minorities," said Akali Dal spokesman Kanwaljit Singh. "I do believe the party has to seek a policy of moderation if it truly wants to govern India."
Sikhs form the majority in Punjab, but constitute only two percent of India's population of 936 million. Hindus comprise 82 percent.

The BJP ruled India for 13 days following inconclusive national elections in May 1996, but failed to hold on to power when it could not muster a majority in the 545-seat Lok Sabha, or lower house of parliament.
"If the BJP changes its policies, it would not be so isolated again," Kanwaljit Singh said, referring to the BJP's hardline Hindu stand on national issues.

"The Hindus dominate the cities. The BJP is their major mouthpiece. Sikhs dominate the countryside. The combination is formidable," said Ashis Nandy, an analyst at the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies in New Delhi.
